title: Force and its Effect
status: draft: written 18 Nov 2026 offline for Grade 4 Science and Technology; not yet checked by a CBC Science and Technology teacher; not loaded by the live tutor
notes: Every idea is shown with a real push or pull: a ball rolled on grass and on cement, a drawer, a stretched rubber band, a magnet with paper clips and coins. The child predicts before each demonstration.

skills.key_step: The child names the force in a situation (push, pull, gravity, friction, magnetic) and knows non-living things can exert forces.

floor.prerequisite: Knows that pushing and pulling move things.
floor.question: Do you push or pull to open a drawer?

representations: a drawer, a door and a wheelbarrow
a magnet with pins, coins and paper clips
a table: action and type of force
steps: Push: away from you. Pull: towards you.
Gravity: everything is pulled down to the Earth.
Friction: rubbing surfaces slow things down.
Magnetic: magnets pull iron things, not all metals.
contexts: pushing a wheelbarrow on a farm
a mango falling from a tree

board.do: Draw a mango tree with a mango falling.
Wait for the child to say gravity.
Ask whether a magnet will pick up a five-shilling coin.

listen_for: opening a drawer is a push
misconceptions.ask: Is the drawer coming towards you or going away?
misconceptions.repair: Towards you is a pull; away is a push.

misconceptions.ask: Did the magnet lift the aluminium sufuria lid?
misconceptions.repair: Magnets attract iron and steel, not all metals.

listen_for: gravity only works when it falls
misconceptions.ask: Why does a book stay on the table and not float up?
misconceptions.repair: Gravity pulls on everything all the time.

misconceptions.ask: Who pulled the pins to the magnet?
misconceptions.repair: Non-living things like magnets and the Earth exert forces.

checks.question: What type of force makes a stone fall to the ground?
A magnet is held near an iron nail and a copper wire. Which one moves?

skills.key_step: The child says a force can start movement, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction and change an object's shape.

floor.question: Is kicking a ball a push or a pull?

representations: a football kicked, stopped and turned
a table of effects with an example each
steps: Direction: hit a moving ball sideways.
Shape: squeeze plasticine or a sponge.
contexts: a ball rolling on the school field

board.do: Draw a ball rolling to the right.
Draw a foot hitting it from the side.
Ask which way the ball will go now.

misconceptions.ask: What does the goalkeeper do to the ball?
misconceptions.repair: A force can also stop movement or change its direction.

listen_for: squeezing is not a force effect
misconceptions.ask: What changed the shape of the dough?
misconceptions.repair: Changing shape is an effect of a force.

misconceptions.ask: After the kick, is the foot still touching the ball?
misconceptions.repair: A ball keeps moving after the kick until a force such as friction stops it.

misconceptions.ask: Where does the ball roll further: on grass or on cement?
misconceptions.repair: Friction is a force that slows and stops the ball.

checks.question: Name two effects of a force on a ball.
checks.answer: any two: start it, stop it, speed up, slow down, change direction, change shape

checks.question: What effect does a force have when you squeeze a lump of clay?

skills.key_step: The child gives everyday uses of forces, including small ones (writing, walking) and useful friction and gravity, and knows each task needs the right amount of force.

floor.prerequisite: Can say the effects of a force.
floor.question: What can a force do to a moving ball?
floor.answer: stop it, slow it or change its direction

representations: shoes with and without grip on a smooth floor
steps: List tasks in a day: walking, writing, lifting, cycling.
Find a use of friction (grip, brakes) and of gravity (pouring, falling rain).
Say how much force each needs.

board.do: Draw a shoe sole with grooves.
Wait for the child to say grip or friction.

misconceptions.ask: What would happen to walking on a floor with no friction?
misconceptions.repair: Friction helps us walk, write and brake.

misconceptions.ask: How would you pour water without gravity?
misconceptions.repair: Gravity is useful: water flows down, rain falls, things stay on tables.

listen_for: writing is not using a force
misconceptions.ask: What does your hand do to the pencil?
misconceptions.repair: Small tasks such as writing and walking use force too.

misconceptions.ask: What happens to the pencil point if you press very hard?
misconceptions.repair: Each task needs the right amount of force.

checks.question: Give one use of friction in daily life.
checks.answer: walking without slipping, brakes, writing, striking a match

checks.question: How does gravity help when fetching water from a tank?
checks.answer: it makes the water flow down out of the tap
